sources.title: Lesya Ukrainka (Q298033), verified live via the Wikidata API (2026-11-13): English label 'Lesya Ukrainka', description 'Ukrainian poet, writer and feminist (1871-1913)', instance of human, born 13 February (Julian) / 25 February 1871, died 1 August 1913, Korean label 레샤 우크라인카. Orientation only; not used as support for any row.

Petro Odarchenko, 'Ukrainka, Lesia', Internet Encyclopedia of Ukraine (Canadian Institute of Ukrainian Studies; first printed in the Encyclopedia of Ukraine, vol. 5, 1993; read in full with its bibliography). CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: poet and playwright (pseudonym of Larysa Kosach-Kvitka, 1871-1913) who reached her literary heights in the 'dramatic poem', a genre she developed, beginning with Oderzhyma (1901); her best-known dramatic works include The Stone Host, Cassandra, The Boyar Woman, In the Catacombs and the neoromantic Forest Song (1911); first poems in Zoria (Lviv, 1884), collections Na krylakh pisen (1893), Dumy i mriyi (1899), Vidhuky (1902); translations of Gogol, Mickiewicz, Heine, Hugo and Homer, the Heine Book of Songs translated with Maksym Slavinsky (1892); self-educated, a history textbook for her sisters at 19; member of the Pleiada literary group in Kyiv; the Babylonian-captivity dramatic poems read as symbols of Ukrainian subjection. Scholarly reference entry by a literary historian, admiring in tone; the illness it also notes is not used for any row.

Roma Franko (sketch), edited by Sonia Morris, 'Lesya Ukrainka (1871-1913): Biographical Sketch', Language Lanterns Publications, 1998 (publisher's page, read in full). Educational biography: Ukrainian-language home education by tutors, languages learned (Russian, Polish, Bulgarian, Greek, Latin, French, Italian, German, English), the Pleiades circle organised with her brother Mykhailo at seventeen, her uncle Mykhailo Drahomanov encouraging her to collect folk songs and study history and the Bible, the Heine translation (1892) and first collection (1893) printed in Western Ukraine and smuggled into Kyiv because Ukrainian publications were banned in the Russian Empire, her correspondence with Olha Kobylianska, marriage in 1907 to the ethnographer Klyment Kvitka who transcribed and published the folk songs she knew. Publisher biography for a translation series.

Christine Chraibi, 'The many faces of Ukrainian writer & feminist Lesia Ukrainka', Euromaidan Press, 25 March 2020 (read in full). Popular online biography: the Pleiada circle founded in 1888 with her brother, her membership in the Kyiv Literary and Artistic Society (1895-97), her collecting and performing of folk songs, a history manual written at 19, one impromptu poem in Russian, her marriage in 1907 to Klyment Kvitka against her mother's opposition after renouncing family financial help (single-source claim), and her 1891 letter from Vienna on Austrian freedom compared with the Russian Empire. Popular-press source that repeats family-memoir material; some health details in it are not used.

Halyna Tereshchuk, 'Dvi lyubovni dramy: u Lvovi prezentuvaly fotohrafiyu Lesi Ukrainky 1901 roku' (Radio Svoboda, 25 February 2021; read in full, in Ukrainian). Report on the exhibition of her 1901 Chernivtsi photograph at the Ivan Franko literary-memorial museum in Lviv (with comments from the museum director Bohdan Tykholoz, the researcher Tamara Skrypka and her husband Klyment Kvitka's recollection that she found the photograph truest to her) and on Ivan Trush's 1900 portrait of her: sittings in Kyiv for the Shevchenko Scientific Society, Trush's sale of the replica to Count Leon Pininsky, her insistence in 1903 that the replica be destroyed, and her breaking off contact with him when he refused. Journalism with museum-side voices.

Lesya Ukrainka Portal (lesyaukrainka.com), entry 'Trush I. Lesya Ukrainka (portrait)' in the section on Lesya Ukrainka in the visual arts (read in full, in Ukrainian). Research-portal note: the 1900 portrait painted by Ivan Trush as part of the Shevchenko Scientific Society's gallery of Ukrainian figures, sittings in late March and early April 1900 in a temporary studio in the Kyiv museum, first shown in Lviv in June 1901, her guarded reaction, the dispute over the unauthorised sale and the replica; says one version is now in the National Museum in Lviv and the other in the National Art Museum of Ukraine in Kyiv. Used for the portrait record and the 1903 dispute; shares its account with the Radio Svoboda report.

creative_originality.rationale: [src_lesya_eou, src_lesya_languagelanterns | 1896-1912 | scholarly reference entry, publisher biography] The encyclopedia entry says she developed a new genre, the 'dramatic poem', beginning with Oderzhyma (1901), and reached her literary heights in it, applying the form to biblical, classical and Ukrainian material; the publisher sketch calls the pithy philosophical dramatic poems her greatest legacy. CONCENTRATION (agent): lowered from 70 / 0.54 (strong_inference) because the genre claim rests mainly on one literary-historical entry and the second source states the same assessment without detail, so it is closer to a critical judgment than to two documented instances.

cross_domain_range.rationale: [src_lesya_eou, src_lesya_languagelanterns, src_lesya_euromaidan | 1885-1912 | scholarly reference entry, publisher biography, popular biography] Documented work in lyric poetry, dramatic poems, prose, literary criticism and sociopolitical essays, translation from several languages, a history textbook written at 19 and the collecting of folk songs. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 66 / 0.52 because almost all of it lies within literature and related written work, and the three accounts repeat the same list.

curiosity.rationale: [src_lesya_eou, src_lesya_languagelanterns, src_lesya_euromaidan | 1880s-1900s | scholarly reference entry, publisher biography, popular biography] The sources agree that she educated herself widely, learned many languages (Russian, Polish, Bulgarian, Greek, Latin and Western European languages), wrote a history textbook at 19 and, on her uncle Drahomanov's urging, collected folk songs and studied history and the Bible. CONCENTRATION (agent): lowered from 68 / 0.52 (strong_inference) because the three sources retell the same biographical facts, the home-education and her uncle's encouragement are described as family-supplied, and none describes how she pursued questions.

collaboration.rationale: [src_lesya_eou, src_lesya_languagelanterns, src_lesya_euromaidan | 1885-1907 | scholarly reference entry, publisher biography, popular biography] She translated Gogol with her brother Mykhailo (1885) and Heine with Maksym Slavinsky (1892), took part in the Pleiada circle, corresponded closely with Olha Kobylianska, and her husband Klyment Kvitka transcribed and published the folk songs she knew. CONCENTRATION (agent): lowered from 62 / 0.50 (strong_inference) because the three accounts are one biographical tradition and the cooperative episodes are listed, not described in detail.

proactive_agency.rationale: [src_lesya_languagelanterns, src_lesya_euromaidan, src_lesya_eou | 1888-1895 | publisher biography, popular biography, scholarly reference entry] The publisher sketch and the popular biography say that at 17 she and her brother organised the Pleiada circle to promote Ukrainian literature and translate world classics, but the encyclopedia entry says only that she joined it, so the sources disagree on her role. CONCENTRATION (agent): lowered from 62 / 0.48 because of that disagreement and because the organising claim comes from the two secondary retellings.

impact_motivation.rationale: [src_lesya_eou, src_lesya_languagelanterns | 1893-1910 | scholarly reference entry, publisher biography] The encyclopedia entry reads her dramatic poems on captives in Babylon and on Cassandra and the Boyar Woman as addressed to Ukrainian passivity and imprisonment in the Russian Empire, and the publisher sketch says her first books had to be printed in Western Ukraine and smuggled into Kyiv. CONCENTRATION (agent): lowered from 64 / 0.46 because the claim is the entry's interpretation of her works, not a documented act of her own, and the smuggling account is secondary.

conflict_tolerance.rationale: [src_lesya_radiosvoboda, src_lesya_portal | 1903 | press report, research portal] When Ivan Trush sold a replica of her portrait to a private collector, she insisted in 1903 that it be destroyed and, when he refused, broke off contact with him (museum director's account in the press report; the portal says she was angered by the unauthorised sale). SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 60 / 0.42 because it is one episode, told in the same museum-side narrative by both sources. Impact is dual-edged: it cost her the friendship.

autonomy_need.rationale: [src_lesya_euromaidan, src_lesya_languagelanterns | 1907 | popular biography, publisher biography] The popular biography says she married Klyment Kvitka in 1907 although her mother opposed it and that she renounced family financial help; the publisher sketch confirms the 1907 marriage but not the opposition. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 60 / 0.40 because the key claim comes from one popular article and concerns private life.

portrait.source: Oil portrait of Lesya Ukrainka by Ivan Trush (1900), painted from life in sittings in Kyiv for the Shevchenko Scientific Society (documented by the Lesya Ukrainka Portal and Radio Svoboda); Wikimedia Commons file 'Портрет Лесі Українки (Іван Труш).jpg' (a 2021 photograph of the painting as shown in the exhibition 'Lesya Ukrainka: 150 names' at the Ukrainian House, Kyiv; Commons and Wikidata name the National Museum in Lviv as holder). The Commons original (3430 x 4573) was downscaled to 750 x 1000; no upscaling.
portrait.license: Public domain: the artist Ivan Trush died in 1941 (life plus 70 years expired in 2011; also published before 1931 for the United States); a faithful photograph of a two-dimensional public-domain painting adds no new copyright (Commons tag PD-Art). The holder's own item record could not be found online, so no holder terms were read.
portrait.attribution: Ivan Trush, Portrait of Lesya Ukrainka, 1900, oil on panel; photograph by Rasal Hague (Wikimedia Commons, 2021), downscaled.
portrait.creator: Ivan Trush (1869-1941)

provenance.notes: QID VERIFIED LIVE (2026-11-13, Wikidata API) Q298033 'Lesya Ukrainka', 'Ukrainian poet, writer and feminist (1871-1913)', human, born 1871-02-13/25 (Julian/Gregorian), died 1913-07-19/08-01, ko label 레샤 우크라인카. REGION central_europe (Ukrainian precedent Taras Shevchenko; no eastern_europe id exists), ERA 20th_century (mature work 1899-1913), nationality UA. NO HEALTH SCORING: her documented illness is noted in sources but no row, card or interpretation rests on it or on any diagnosis. ZERO POLITICS: only writing, translation, circle-founding and a personal dispute are scored; the sources' nationalist and feminist framing is context, not scored. ATTRIBUTION: attributable. CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: Odarchenko in the Internet Encyclopedia of Ukraine. READ (5 besides Wikidata): EoU entry, Language Lanterns sketch, Euromaidan Press article, Radio Svoboda report, Lesya Ukrainka Portal Trush page; also read but not cited: a podcast transcript (inaccurate in places), Google Arts and Culture story, Zaxid.net report. Sparse 8-row profile; all biographical sources share one family-memoir tradition, so five rows were lowered for concentration and three in self-calibration (see handback). Conflict: EoU says she joined Pleiada, two secondary sources say she organised it; Pleiada dates and the Heine translation year (1892 vs 1893) vary and are not carded. portrait_preflight: plausible (lead) / REPLACED: the lead's 1901 Krzanowski photograph (Commons 'Lesya Ukrainka 1901 (facecrop).jpg', PD-old-70-1923) was NOT used: the photographer Jan Krzanowski (Chernivtsi atelier) has no death date, the original is held by the Ivan Franko museum in Lviv (acquired from a private collection in 2001, first exhibited 2021) and no holder rights record is available, so its public-domain status cannot be verified. The 1908 'Ukrainian Muza' anthology plate (Kyiv, Commons PD) was also checked: it carries the printed heading 'Lesya Ukrainka' but is a coarse line reproduction. Replacement is Ivan Trush's 1900 oil portrait, painted from life (sittings March-April 1900). Caveats: two versions exist (Lviv and Kyiv museums) and sources disagree which is the original; Commons names Lviv for the photographed one; holder item record not found online; image is a tight crop of an exhibition photograph. Identity is not in doubt (titled portrait of her, documented commission).
